newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-TYSON TO LEARN HIS FATE ON WEDNESDAY.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-TYSON TO LEARN HIS FATE ON WEDNESDAY.

text.p: Former world heavyweight champion Mike Tyson's boxing future will be decided in Las Vegas Wednesday by five men who could ban him for life, suspend him for a while, or fine him millions of dollars.

With almost everyone, from the president of the United States down, expressing horror after Tyson was disqualified for biting Evander Holyfield's ears in their June 28 fight, there is pressure on the Nevada State Athletic Commission to come down hard on the fighter.
Holyfield himself, although forgiving Tyson for the bites, has called for his opponent to be banned from boxing for at least two years.

In a TV interview before he left on a trip to South Africa, the champion said the Nevada officials have a chance to make a decision that will, "make all the fighters never, ever want to do anything like that.
"Let's get the whole game of boxing to make a pitch to be better," he pleaded.
Asked if he thought Tyson's suspension should be at least two years, he said, "yeah, that or more because you (only) fight once or twice a year usually."
Fight promoter Bob Arum, a rival of Don King, who promoted the Tyson-Holyfield rematch, referred to President Clinton's comment that he and most Americans were "horrified" at Tyson's behaviour.
"The Nevada Athletic Commission has got to do the right thing," Arum told the Las Vegas Review-Journal. "It holds the future of the sport of boxing in its hands."
King, who is not often shy in talking, has been unusually reticent about the case, but is widely believed to have orchestrated Tyson's public apology two days after the fight.

In what was seen by boxing insiders as a calculated appeal for mercy, a contrite Tyson apologised for "snapping" in the ring and said he would accept whatever punishment the commission decided. But he also appealed against a life ban.

At an emergency meeting of the commission last week, Tyson's lawyer said the fighter waived his right to a 30-day notice of a disciplinary hearing and would accept the commission's decision. He said he did not know if Tyson would attend Wednesday's hearing.
The five-man commission temporarily suspended Tyson last week and froze his $30 million purse for the fight.
Under current rules, the commission, which regulates boxing in Nevada, could suspend Tyson, it could withhold 10 percent of his purse or it could revoke his boxing license.

Under new federal laws, a suspension in Nevada could effectively bar Tyson from fighting anywhere in the United States. The law does not force other states to honour a Nevada ban, but states such as New Jersey or California would have to justify allowing him to fight in their jurisdictions.
Officials in Nevada, where boxing goes hand-in-hand with the gaming industry as an important source of state revenue, have urged the Athletic Commission to send a strong message.

State Attorney General Frankie Sue Del Pappa called Tuesday for Tyson's boxing license to be completely revoked and the same day the Nevada legislature passed a bill under which a boxer would forfeit the whole purse for illegal acts in the ring.

However, the bill, which specifies ear-biting among illegal acts in boxing, would not be retroactive, so could not be used in the Tyson-Holyfield case. Nevada Gov. Bob Miller said he will sign the bill into law.

An indication of how important boxing is to the economy of Nevada is that the state took in more than $570,000 in taxes on gross ticket sales for the June 28 fight, as well as $50,000 in TV fees. And title fights attract more business to the Las Vegas and Reno casinos.
Tyson himself has already suffered repercussions for the bites. The World Boxing Association stripped him Tuesday of his ranking.

Tyson, who until the ill-fated title fight occupied the number one challenger spot behind Holyfield, could be re-assigned a ranking after completing any suspension handed down by the Nevada commission, the Caracas-based WBA said.
